lines.text: When Grandpa Omar was five years old, he rode a small red tricycle around his neighborhood.
Riding outside every afternoon was a regular habit, but he stopped riding it as he grew older.
In the past, daily life looked very different before modern computers and smartphones arrived.
People used to play their favorite music on plastic tape cassettes.
In those days, families listened to the morning news together on tabletop radios.
Drivers could not look at digital touchscreens, so they opened large paper maps to find their way across town.
Instead of sending instant text messages, people mailed handwritten letters to their friends and relatives.
A past situation can be a repeated action or a personal condition that lasted for a long time.
In English grammar, when we talk about these past routines, we always follow "used to" with the base form of the main verb.
If an action did not happen, we say that someone didn't use to do it.
When asking a question with "Did you," we drop the letter "d" and write use to keep the sentence correct.
All of these old habits are no longer true today, but remembering them helps us understand how our daily routines change over time.
People didn't use to carry smartphones.
Did you use to ride a tricycle?
